extracted.intended_audience: entrepreneurs, startup founders, small-business owners, and PR/marketing people responsible for writing and sending company launch (new business) press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Practical step-by-step guidance for creating and pitching a press release announcing a new business or company launch, including story framing, required press-release components, media targeting, and longer-term PR strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think of an inspirational brand-driven story for your new business
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a press release, don’t focus on the best features of your product or the details of the service. Instead, write a press release about a problem or a need that your company’s product will provide a solution to. Think of a catchy topic for the media in the context of your new business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight what makes the brand story interesting to readers and journalists — e.g., the CEO’s exceptional personality or experience, or a different offering in a monopolized market (example: Juul defining itself as a distinctive 'smoking alternative'). Avoid product-feature lists; lead with the problem/solution narrative that journalists and audiences will care about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the press release simple and non-technical
rubrics_metrics.description: The new business press release shouldn’t be too long or too technical. Beware the 'curse of knowledge' where founders assume domain knowledge and fail to explain simply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in plain language that anyone (including non-experts) can understand. Avoid jargon and unnecessary technical detail. Keep length concise and prioritise clarity over exhaustive technical descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the standard press release structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the new business press release format: Headline, Lead, Dateline, Body, Company details, Media contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this conventional structure because it's what journalists expect and helps them quickly identify newsworthiness and necessary facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline — attention-grabbing and launch-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline – an attention-grabbing headline about your company launch. Make it count!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a concise, newsy headline that emphasizes the most compelling angle of the launch; avoid vague or overly promotional phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead — answer who, what, when, why, and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead – a brief overview of the whole story, including answers to the questions: Who? What? When? Why? With what effect?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the key facts and news hook in the lead so journalists immediately understand the essence and significance of the announcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline — confirm timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline – to confirm that you’re providing the most up-to-date information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an appropriate dateline (city and date) to signal recency and context for the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body — order from most newsworthy to secondary details
rubrics_metrics.description: Body – an explanation of the information provided earlier in the lead, starting from the most newsworthy info about your product and finishing with secondary details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inverted-pyramid ordering: expand on the lead, add supporting details, quotes, and relevant context, and leave background or technical minutiae toward the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company details — short descriptive paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Company details – a short paragraph about your company and its products to help journalists understand the nature of the business and make writing about it easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise boilerplate that explains what the company does, its mission, and quick facts journalists can reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information — provide clear contact details
rubrics_metrics.description: Media contact information – the author's or company’s/agency’s contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include name, email, phone number and any PR representative details so journalists can quickly follow up for interviews or clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch to relevant journalists (targeted outreach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A key factor in getting your press release picked up by the media is pitching to relevant journalists and bloggers—people that are interested in writing about your type of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build or use media lists filtered by industry and location; avoid the 'spray and pray' method of sending releases to everyone. Target journalists whose beats match your business and story angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research journalists’ beats and interests
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re writing a press release about a business that specialises in natural cosmetics, check which journalists are actually interested in natural and organic products, and not just cosmetics in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check past coverage to ensure a journalist will care about your angle. Journalists are usually interested in new pieces of information they have not heard of, or ideas and theories that challenge current beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalise your pitch to the journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: When pitching a journalist, bringing up what they wrote about or other small details about them can go a long way. And at the very least—include their name in the email instead of using a generic email greeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference the journalist's recent work, use their name, and tailor the pitch to their beat; personalisation improves pickup chances vs. generic mass emails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define a long-term communications strategy and PR outreach plan
rubrics_metrics.description: There are so many topics you can cover, which is why having a clear PR outreach plan for each news, backed by an actual communications strategy, can really pay off in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan ongoing storylines (e.g., first client wins, international partnerships, branch openings), prepare follow-up pitches, and align releases with broader business milestones and contractual permissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure contractual rights to use client names or claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If you land a client who is a big and well-known company, guarantee yourself the right to use that fact in the contract before you publicise it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm permissions in writing before mentioning clients, partners or contractual details in press materials to avoid legal/relationship problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain clearly why your business is newsworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Include information on why your business is worth writing about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly call out the news hook — innovations, firsts, notable hires, client wins, market differentiation — so journalists understand the public-interest angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AI tools to generate and refine the press release (follow the tool’s workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-powered tools can help create drafts, provide advanced editing suggestions, and recommend who to send your press release to. Prowly’s workflow: select type and audience, choose language, enter key messages, answer follow-up questions, then customise and edit the draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using AI, be specific with inputs: provide unique value proposition, target market/audience, and team expertise. Answer follow-up questions to make the draft journalist-ready (Prowly’s AI asks ten tailored questions). Edit formatting and tone, and use the AI Assistant's suggestions (it reviews drafts against '11 key criteria') before sending. Also use AI contact recommendations but verify journalist fit manually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear key messages as inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Be as specific as possible and ensure that whatever you choose is the most relevant information about your new business announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested key messages include: Unique Value Proposition (what makes you unique and how you solve a problem), Target Market and Audience (who your ideal customers are), and Team and Expertise (relevant experience and qualifications). These help shape a concise, newsworthy draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and answer journalists’ follow-up questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prowly’s AI will ask more in-depth questions designed to mirror a natural conversation with the journalists you’re targeting — you’ll receive ten questions tailored to the content you shared earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answering likely follow-ups in advance reduces the need for additional back-and-forth and makes it easier for journalists to cover the story quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customise and edit the generated draft before sending
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether you've generated a press release draft or written it yourself, you can adjust header font styles, fine-tune the content, adjust press release length, and put it into a format you're happy with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not send AI output verbatim; tailor tone, length and formatting to the target publication and journalist. Use the editor and AI suggestions to fix weak points and ensure the release matches journalistic expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AI-suggested contact recommendations but validate them
rubrics_metrics.description: Prowly’s AI will suggest journalists you can pitch to based on the keywords found in your press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AI recommendations as a starting point; always check whether each suggested contact has actually covered similar topics and currently covers that beat before pitching.
